001_moby_dick_opening.intro: Five devices in three lines, in reading order.

steps.note: 'Call me Ishmael. Some years ago…' — two statements side by side with no connective. The reader supplies the link between naming and story, and a supplied link is believed.
'—never mind how long precisely—' interrupts the sentence to refuse a fact. The refusal characterizes: a man for whom the years blurred.

'Little or no money,' 'nothing particular' — understatement by negation. The narrator admits poverty and aimlessness while sounding amused by both; the double negative slows the reading at the exact spot he'd rather not dwell on.
The opening is clipped and connective-free; then the ands multiply: 'and nothing particular… and see…' Decisiveness loosens into drift, carried entirely by the conjunctions.
'The watery part of the world' holds the sentence's final position — the stress point in English prose. Everything before it is given information; the sea arrives last, as the new thing.

001_moby_dick_opening.coda: Command, hedge, evasion, drift, horizon — five gestures in forty-five words, none stated, all performed.

003_tale_two_cities_opening.intro: Ten clauses, one famous comma splice.

steps.note: 'It was the' — ten times. The fixed frame drives all attention to the one slot that changes.

Each pair sets opposites in identical grammar: best against worst, Light against Darkness, hope against despair. The symmetry weighs the contraries equally — the sentence refuses to choose, and that refusal is the novel's thesis.
Each clause runs copula, article, noun, 'of,' noun, at near-equal length. The metrical match makes the oppositions toll rather than alternate.
Everything and its opposite, asserted of the same moment. Not a contradiction to resolve but a condition to inhabit: revolutionary time, performed rather than described.
Ten independent clauses joined by commas — normally an error. The splice enforces breathlessness: full stops would let the reader rest, and rest would let the reader choose sides.

003_tale_two_cities_opening.coda: One pattern repeated past prudence, carrying a historical argument. Repetition without escalation is a metronome; here the escalation happens in the reader.

005_hamlet_to_be.intro: The most famous sentence fragment in English: the question never completes, and the incompletion is the character.

steps.note: 'To be, or not to be' — infinitives without a subject. Hamlet contemplates existence without attaching it to himself; the grammar holds the question at arm's length.
To suffer (passive) against to take arms (active), in balanced frames. The scales are loaded: quiet dignity on one side, doomed grandeur on the other.
'The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune' — suffering as bombardment. Slings and arrows are aimed: fortune, in this figure, is not indifferent but hostile.

'To take arms against a sea of troubles.' Swords are useless against water — which is the point. The broken figure diagnoses the plan: the contemplated action is as impossible as the image that carries it.
'Whether 'tis nobler…' opens a subordinate clause that waits for a main clause that never comes. The sentence cannot decide; neither can he.

005_hamlet_to_be.coda: Syntax is character: what the mind cannot do, its grammar cannot do.

026_declaration_independence.intro: One sentence built to make an arguable proposition sound like arithmetic.

steps.note: 'We hold' — not 'we believe,' which invites dispute, nor 'we assert,' which admits effort. To hold a truth is to possess it already. And 'we' recruits every reader into a body that never convened.
'Self-evident' omits the entire case: truths requiring no proof receive none. The reader, credited with finding them obvious, declines to ask for evidence.

'That all men… that they are endowed… that among these are.' Three claims hung from one verb by one repeated word — clauses of a single contract rather than three separate assertions, each separately deniable.
'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' ascends from bare existence to freedom to — not happiness — its pursuit. The final term is carefully unpromised.

'Are created… are endowed' — passive with the agent named: 'by their Creator.' The construction puts men in the subject position and their rights at the point of stress. Compare the agentless passive of the press release.

026_declaration_independence.coda: Style here is not the decoration of the argument. It is the argument.

027_gettysburg_address.intro: The opening sentence does half the speech's work: consecrate the ground, refound the nation.

steps.note: 'Four score and seven' where 'eighty-seven' would do. The number arrives already antique, already scriptural — consecration does not happen in invoice language.
The cadence is cut to the pattern of Genesis and the Psalms. The audience carried one book in common; the sentence borrows that book's authority without citing it.
The nation is 'conceived' and 'brought forth' — a birth, with Liberty as its condition. Nations that are born can die, and can be reborn: the figure plants the speech's conclusion.
'Conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition' — two participles in step, origin as condition and vow. 'A new birth of freedom' later redeems exactly this parallel.
'All men are created equal' — Jefferson, verbatim, unattributed. The quotation reframes the Declaration as a 'proposition' still to be proven, on that field.

027_gettysburg_address.coda: No ornament, no digression: every device serves the single motion from past birth to present test.

028_i_have_dream.intro: The most famous anaphora in American English — and the frame is the least of it.

steps.note: 'I have a dream' — present tense, first person, possessive. The dream exists now, in a particular man, as a fact no vote can repeal.
The frame returns and each return raises the cargo: the nation, the states, his own children. Anaphora as ratchet — same words, higher price each time.
'This nation will rise up' — will, not may. Prophecy, not proposal: certainty stated until the audience supplies it.
Jefferson quoted in full, on the steps of Lincoln's memorial: the founding sentence read back to the nation as an unpaid promissory note.
The colon presents the creed as evidence — exhibit A, entered into the record. The dream is only that the country honor its own signed words.

028_i_have_dream.coda: Old devices, new aim: every figure points the nation's own language back at it.

082_one_art.intro: A poem about losing everything, in the tone of someone teaching a card trick. The gap between tone and freight is the poem.

steps.note: 'The art of losing' — the verb of catastrophe nominalized into a discipline. Arts are chosen; the grammar quietly claims loss can be practiced.
'Isn't hard to master,' 'no disaster' — negation naming the exact words, hard and disaster, that the speaker is trying not to believe.
The claim is instruction; the truth is grief. Reader and speaker both know 'isn't hard to master' is false — the poem shows a lie being practiced with perfect technique.
Things 'filled with the intent to be lost.' If objects intend their loss, no one loses them: agency transferred, the speaker briefly not responsible.
'Their loss is no disaster' lands like a verdict — then four stanzas re-test it against larger and larger losses until it cracks. An opening statement, not a conclusion.

082_one_art.coda: No exclamation, no weeping — only grammar arranged to keep the speaker upright. That is what understatement is for.

090_blood_meridian.intro: Two sentences: three words, then forty. The ratio is the style.

steps.note: 'They rode on.' Complete, closed. The second sentence opens its floodgate with no transition — violence stated flatly, cosmology unspooling after.
'They rode… They rode' — the smallest possible anaphora, returning across the novel like hoofbeats. Flat repetition, no crescendo: persistence like weather.
'Antique and diffuse and the wholes thereof' — the ands refuse hierarchy. Nothing subordinated, everything level; the sentence rides on because the syntax will not stop.
'The wholes thereof' — King James diction. The archaism grants a band of scalp-hunters the cadence of prophecy and turns the desert into Old Testament ground.
After the biblical machinery: 'scattered like paper in the wind.' Not chaff, not stars — paper. The grand purpose compares, in the end, to litter.

090_blood_meridian.coda: Three beats, then forty — prose scored, not merely written.
